claim: Unipolar brush cells (UBCs) are excitatory interneurons in the cerebellar cortex that receive mossy fiber (MF) inputs and excite granule cells.
source: Unipolar brush cells (UBCs) are excitatory interneurons in the cerebellar cortex that receive mossy fiber (MF) inputs and excite granule cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the basic identity and connectivity of UBCs.

claim: The UBC population responds to brief burst activation of MFs with a continuum of temporal transformations.
source: The UBC population responds to brief burst activation of MFs with a continuum of temporal transformations, but it is not known how UBCs transform the diverse range of MF input patterns that occur in vivo.
evidence: This statement is made in the abstract and is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: AMPARs transmit timing information for single stimuli at up to 5 spikes/s, and for very brief bursts.
source: AMPARs transmit timing information for single stimuli at up to 5 spikes/s, and for very brief bursts.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: A combination of mGluR2/3s (inhibitory) and mGluR1s (excitatory) mediates a continuum of delayed, and broadened responses to longer bursts, and to sustained high frequency activation.
source: A combination of mGluR2/3s (inhibitory) and mGluR1s (excitatory) mediates a continuum of delayed, and broadened responses to longer bursts, and to sustained high frequency activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological experiments in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Variability in the mGluR2/3 component controls the time course of the onset of firing.
source: Variability in the mGluR2/3 component controls the time course of the onset of firing, and variability in the mGluR1 component controls the duration of prolonged firing.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by the pharmacological experiments showing that blocking mGluR2/3 affects the delay in UBC responses.

claim: Variability in the mGluR1 component controls the duration of prolonged firing.
source: Variability in the mGluR2/3 component controls the time course of the onset of firing, and variability in the mGluR1 component controls the duration of prolonged firing.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological experiments showing that mGluR1 mediates long-lasting responses.

claim: The combination of glutamate receptor types allows each UBC to simultaneously convey different aspects of MF firing.
source: We conclude that the combination of glutamate receptor types allows each UBC to simultaneously convey different aspects of MF firing.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental data showing distinct contributions of different receptor types.

claim: UBCs are highly flexible circuit elements that provide diverse temporal transformations that are well suited to contribute to specialized processing in different regions of the cerebellar cortex.
source: These findings establish that UBCs are highly flexible circuit elements that provide diverse temporal transformations that are well suited to contribute to specialized processing in different regions of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: UBCs receive a single mossy fiber (MF) input onto their large dendritic brush.
source: They receive a single mossy fiber (MF) input onto their large dendritic brush, and they in turn make their own mossy fiber boutons that make synapse mainly onto granule cells, but also onto other UBCs (Rossi et al., 1995; Nunzi et al., 2001; Hariani et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: UBCs make their own mossy fiber boutons that make synapse mainly onto granule cells, but also onto other UBCs.
source: They receive a single mossy fiber (MF) input onto their large dendritic brush, and they in turn make their own mossy fiber boutons that make synapse mainly onto granule cells, but also onto other UBCs (Rossi et al., 1995; Nunzi et al., 2001; Hariani et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: UBCs transform MF firing patterns into prolonged increases or decreases in firing that lead to diverse granule cell firing patterns.
source: UBCs transform MF firing patterns into prolonged increases or decreases in firing that lead to diverse granule cell firing patterns (Rossi et al., 1995; Kinney et al., 1997; Diño et al., 2000; Mugnaini et al., 2011; Locatelli et al., 2013; Kennedy et al., 2014; van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014; Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015; Zampini et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: In weakly electric fish, UBC firing provides a filtered signal that is suited to cancelling self-generated signals.
source: In weakly electric fish, UBC firing provides a filtered signal that is suited to cancelling self-generated signals (Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In the absence of simultaneous recordings from connected MF-UBC pairs it is not known how UBCs transform MF firing patterns during behaviors.
source: In the rodent brain, recordings have been made from UBCs in vivo (Simpson et al., 2005; Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008; Ruigrok et al., 2011; Hensbroek et al., 2015; Witter and De Zeeuw, 2015), but in the absence of simultaneous recordings from connected MF-UBC pairs it is not known how UBCs transform MF firing patterns during behaviors.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge in the introduction.

claim: UBCs responses range from fast 'ON' cells that fire for hundreds of milliseconds with virtually no delay, to intermediate UBCs that initially pause before increasing firing for seconds, to 'OFF' UBCs that suppress firing for up to two seconds.
source: UBCs responses range from fast 'ON' cells that fire for hundreds of milliseconds with virtually no delay, to intermediate UBCs that initially pause before increasing firing for seconds, to 'OFF' UBCs that suppress firing for up to two seconds (Guo et al., 2021a; Huson et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: mGluR2/3s activate potassium channels to suppress firing.
source: mGluR2/3s activate potassium channels to suppress firing (Russo et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2012; Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015), while a combination of AMPARs and mGluR1s mediate excitation (Rossi et al., 1995; Kinney et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2012; Schwartz et al., 2012; Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015; Guo et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A combination of AMPARs and mGluR1s mediate excitation in UBCs.
source: mGluR2/3s activate potassium channels to suppress firing (Russo et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2012; Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015), while a combination of AMPARs and mGluR1s mediate excitation (Rossi et al., 1995; Kinney et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2012; Schwartz et al., 2012; Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015; Guo et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Populations of UBCs exhibit a continuum of response durations and amplitudes, which is thought to reflect inverse expression profiles of the mGluR1 and mGluR2 signaling pathways.
source: Populations of UBCs exhibit a continuum of response durations and amplitudes, which is thought to reflect inverse expression profiles of the mGluR1 and mGluR2 signaling pathways (Guo et al., 2021a; Kozareva et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: UBCs are present throughout the cerebellar cortex, but they are most abundant in regions involved in the control of eye position and in vestibular processing.
source: Even though UBCs are present throughout the cerebellar cortex, they are most abundant in regions involved in the control of eye position and in vestibular processing (Floris et al., 1994; Diño et al., 1999; Takács et al., 1999; Englund et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MFs in UBC-rich regions often fire in brief high-frequency bursts.
source: MFs in these UBC-rich regions often fire in brief high-frequency bursts (Eccles et al., 1971; van Kan et al., 1993; Garwicz et al., 1998; Rancz et al., 2007) that in some cases represent saccadic eye movements (Ohtsuka and Noda, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MFs can fire continuously for extended periods and change their firing rates dynamically to represent motor signals, and encode velocity, position, and direction.
source: MFs can also fire continuously for extended periods and change their firing rates dynamically to represent motor signals, and encode velocity, position, and direction (Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978; van Kan et al., 1993; Arenz et al., 2008; Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008; Lisberger, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cell-attached recordings from UBCs in acute cerebellar slices were used to examine responses to MF firing patterns based on in vivo recordings.
source: Here, we use cell-attached recordings from UBCs in acute cerebellar slices to examine responses to MF firing patterns that are based on in vivo recordings.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: MFs evoke a continuum of responses in the UBC population.
source: We find that MFs evoke a continuum of responses in the UBC population, mediated by three different types of glutamate receptors that each convey a specialized component.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Three different types of glutamate receptors each convey a specialized component of UBC responses.
source: We find that MFs evoke a continuum of responses in the UBC population, mediated by three different types of glutamate receptors that each convey a specialized component.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological experiments.

claim: In vivo recordings of MF activity were obtained from the floccular complex of rhesus macaques during a smooth pursuit eye movement task.
source: For this purpose, we utilized in vivo recordings of MF activity during a smooth pursuit eye movement task from the floccular complex of rhesus macaques (provided by David J. Herzfeld and Stephen G. Lisberger) and reproduced the firing patterns observed there in acute cerebellar slices (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the source of the in vivo MF firing patterns used in the study.

claim: MF firing is comprised of sustained changes in firing that encode velocity and eye position, burst discharges that encode saccades, or a combination of both.
source: MF firing is comprised of sustained changes in firing that encode velocity and eye position, burst discharges that encode saccades, or a combination of both (Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Cell-attached recordings were performed from UBCs in acute cerebellar brain slices from P30-47 mice in the presence of GABAA, GABAB, and glycine receptor blockers.
source: We performed cell-attached recordings from UBCs in acute cerebellar brain slices from P30-47 mice in the presence of GABAA, GABAB, and glycine receptor blockers (see Methods) and stimulated MF inputs using a theta-glass electrode.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: MF stimulation with an artificial burst of 20 stimuli at 100 spk/s evoked diverse long-lasting changes in firing in UBCs.
source: These stimuli evoked diverse long-lasting changes in firing, with Figure 1b depicting examples of a fast UBC with relatively brief increases in firing, a longer lasting mid-range UBC, a slow UBC with a long-lasting increase in firing, and a UBC that is spontaneously active and transiently stops firing (OFF).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The first representative in vivo MF displayed a series of bursts consisting of 2–23 spikes at very high frequencies.
source: The first representative in vivo MF displayed a series of bursts consisting of 2–23 spikes at very high frequencies (Figure 1c, green trace) in line with previous findings (Eccles et al., 1971; Rancz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1c, with supporting citations.

claim: Different UBCs provided diverse temporal transformations of the in vivo MF input patterns.
source: Overall, the different UBCs provided diverse temporal transformations of the in vivo MF input patterns.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Single stimuli and brief bursts evoked large rapid increases in firing in close to half of the UBCs.
source: Single stimuli and brief bursts evoked large rapid increases in firing in close to half of the UBCs (Figure 2a, cell 20; Figure 2b, most cells #1–40), and, surprisingly, peak firing rates were quite similar for single stimuli and 20 stimuli bursts for many of these UBCs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Peak firing rates were quite similar for single stimuli and 20 stimuli bursts for many UBCs.
source: Single stimuli and brief bursts evoked large rapid increases in firing in close to half of the UBCs (Figure 2a, cell 20; Figure 2b, most cells #1–40), and, surprisingly, peak firing rates were quite similar for single stimuli and 20 stimuli bursts for many of these UBCs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Single stimuli and brief bursts evoked decreases in firing for approximately 20% of the UBCs.
source: Single stimuli and brief bursts evoked decreases in firing for approximately 20% of the UBCs (Figure 2a, cells #55 and #67; Figure 2b, most cells #55–70).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Fast UBCs responded to all burst durations with consistently high peak responses that exceeded 100 spk/s.
source: Fast UBCs responded to all burst durations with consistently high peak responses that exceeded 100 spk/s, while intermediate and slow UBCs increased their peak response almost linearly with burst duration (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Intermediate and slow UBCs increased their peak response almost linearly with burst duration.
source: Fast UBCs responded to all burst durations with consistently high peak responses that exceeded 100 spk/s, while intermediate and slow UBCs increased their peak response almost linearly with burst duration (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The number of spikes evoked by MF stimulation increased with burst duration in almost all cells.
source: The number of spikes evoked by MF stimulation increased with burst duration in almost all cells, but increases were small in fast cells, and could grow more than 100-fold in slow cells (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The half-widths of responses increased with input duration for almost all UBCs, with the largest increases apparent when the number of stimuli increases from one to five.
source: The half-widths of responses also increased with input duration for almost all UBCs, with the largest increases apparent when the number of stimuli increases from one to five (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Fast UBCs are suited to detecting the occurrence of a burst, regardless of burst duration.
source: This suggests that fast UBCs are suited to detecting the occurrence of a bust, regardless of burst duration.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results based on the data showing consistent responses in fast UBCs.

claim: Slow UBCs are suited to detecting bursts of 5–20 MF spikes and scaling their responses proportionally to burst duration.
source: In contrast, slow UBCs are suited to detecting bursts of 5–20 MF spikes and scaling their responses proportionally to burst duration.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results based on the data showing proportional responses in slow UBCs.

claim: NMDARs do not make an appreciable contribution to responses evoked by bursts.
source: NMDARs are also present at UBC synapses, but we found that they do not make an appreciable contribution to responses evoked by bursts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and we therefore did not explicitly examine their contributions in combination with antagonists of the other glutamate receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blocking mGluR2/3 eliminated the pause after MF stimulation.
source: Blocking mGluR2/3 eliminated the pause after MF stimulation (e.g. cell #27, Figure 3a, orange, and Figure 3d, second row), in line with previous findings (Russo et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2012; Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3, with supporting citations.

claim: Blocking mGluR2/3s slightly increased peak responses and the number of evoked spikes in some cells, especially for larger bursts.
source: Blocking mGluR2/3s also slightly increased peak responses (Figure 3b), and the number of evoked spikes in some cells (Figure 3c and e), especially for larger bursts, with significantly more spikes after blocking mGluR2/3s for burst of 5 stimuli or more (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The additional block of AMPARs eliminated increases in firing evoked by single stimuli in most cells.
source: The additional block of AMPARs eliminated increases in firing evoked by single stimuli in most cells (e.g. cell #8, Figure 3a–c, red, and Figure 3d, third row), but its effect diminished with increasing numbers of stimuli in the burst (Figure 3b, c and e), and on average AMPARs were not the main mediator of the increase in firing for bursts of 5 stimuli or more (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: AMPARs were not the main mediator of the increase in firing for bursts of 5 stimuli or more.
source: The additional block of AMPARs eliminated increases in firing evoked by single stimuli in most cells (e.g. cell #8, Figure 3a–c, red, and Figure 3d, third row), but its effect diminished with increasing numbers of stimuli in the burst (Figure 3b, c and e), and on average AMPARs were not the main mediator of the increase in firing for bursts of 5 stimuli or more (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The component of the response that was sensitive to blocking mGluR1 increased as the bursts got longer and was the main mediator of the increase in firing in almost all UBCs for 20 stimulus bursts.
source: The component of the response that was sensitive to blocking mGluR1 increased as the bursts got longer and was the main mediator of the increase in firing in almost all UBCs for 20 stimulus bursts (Figure 3b, c, e and h).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: AMPAR-mediated responses to single stimuli are more common in fast UBCs.
source: AMPAR-mediated responses to single stimuli are more common in fast UBCs (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: AMPAR subunits are expressed homogeneously across within the UBC population.
source: This is surprising since AMPAR subunits are expressed homogeneously across within the UBC population (Guo et al., 2021a; Kozareva et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Each type of glutamate receptor makes a distinct contribution to responses to bursts.
source: In conclusion, each type of glutamate receptor makes a distinct contribution to responses to bursts.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the results based on the pharmacological experiments.

claim: mGluR2/3s mediate pauses in firing for both short and long bursts in over half of the cells.
source: mGluR2/3s mediate pauses in firing for both short and long bursts in over half of the cells.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the results based on the pharmacological experiments.

claim: AMPARs are important mediators of firing rate increases evoked by short bursts in fast UBCs.
source: AMPARs are important mediators of firing rate increases evoked by short bursts in fast UBCs.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the results based on the pharmacological experiments.

claim: mGluR1s are the primary mediators of responses to medium and long duration bursts.
source: mGluR1s are the primary mediators of responses to medium and long duration bursts.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the results based on the pharmacological experiments.

claim: UBCs showed diverse responses to smooth pursuit-like input patterns with prolonged baseline stimulation at 5 spk/s, interposed by 1 s steps to frequencies ranging from 10 to 60 spk/s.
source: UBCs showed diverse responses to this input pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: For some UBCs, each stimulus during 5 spk/s baseline input evoked brief increases in firing, and steps to higher firing rates evoked slower, more prolonged increased in firing.
source: For some UBCs, each stimulus during 5 spk/s baseline input evoked brief increases in firing, and steps to higher firing rates evoked slower, more prolonged increased in firing (Figure 4, cell #4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: UBCs provide both a temporal transformation of sustained changes in firing frequency, and discrete responses evoked by single stimuli.
source: These responses illustrate that UBCs provide both a temporal transformation of sustained changes in firing frequency, and discrete responses evoked by single stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Single stimuli evoked changes in firing in a large percentage of cells for 5 spk/s stimulation, and responses were even larger for 1 spk/s and 2.5 spk/s.
source: Single stimuli evoked changes in firing in a large percentage of cells for 5 spk/s stimulation, and responses were even larger for 1 spk/s and 2.5 spk/s (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 45% of UBCs reduced firing during the 60 spk/s step.
source: The number of evoked spikes that occurred during the 1 s steps increased for fast and intermediate UBCs, while slower UBCs tended to reduce their firing; with 45% of UBCs (14/31) reducing firing during the 60 spk/s step (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4e.

claim: 87% of UBCs fired more spikes after a 60 spk/s step.
source: Step changes more consistently evoked increases in firing in the 3 s after the step, with 87% (27/31) of UBCs firing more spikes after a 60 spk/s step (Figure 4f), leaving only the slowest cells (#28–31) with net decreases in spiking.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Half-decay times of the step responses were highly correlated with the half-widths of the responses to 20 stimuli at 100 spk/s bursts.
source: Half-decay times of the step responses were also highly correlated with the half-widths of the responses to 20 stimuli at 100 spk/s bursts (for the 60 spk/s step: Spearman's Rho = 0.873, p=1.40 × 10–6), and did not consistently change with firing frequency.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a statistical measure.

claim: 33% of cells that showed increases in firing took more than 1 s after the steps for their response amplitude to decay by half.
source: Of the cells that showed increases in firing, 33% (9/27) took more than 1 s after the steps for their response amplitude to decay by half (Figure 4h), causing increases in firing to gradually build during the protocol, such that the response to step to 20 spk/s late in the protocol was far larger than one early in the protocol (e.g. cell #22 and #27, Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4h.

claim: During smooth pursuit-like MF input, fast UBCs closely follow the input pattern, while slow UBCs produce strongly temporally filtered responses.
source: Overall, during smooth pursuit-like MF input, fast UBCs closely follow the input pattern, while slow UBCs produce strongly temporally filtered responses, in line with responses to 20 stimuli at 100 spk/s bursts.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Many UBCs additionally preserve timing information with discrete changes in firing time-locked to lower rate baseline stimuli.
source: However, many UBCs additionally preserve timing information with discrete changes in firing time-locked to lower rate baseline stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Multiple streams of information appear to be simultaneously encoded by the UBC response.
source: As such, multiple streams of information appear to be simultaneously encoded by the response.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: NMDARs do not make an appreciable contribution to responses evoked by smooth pursuit-like stimulus.
source: NMDARs do not make an appreciable contribution to responses evoked by this stimulus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and we therefore did not explicitly examine their contributions in combination with other glutamate-receptor antagonists.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For a fast UBC that responded to each 5 spk/s stimulation and to 1 s increases in input rate, blocking mGluR2/3s had minor effects, while blocking AMPARs eliminated responses to single stimuli only, and blocking mGluR1 eliminated responses to 1 s steps to 10–60 spk/s.
source: For a fast UBC that responded to each 5 spk/s stimulation and to 1 s increases in input rate, blocking mGluR2/3s had minor effects, while blocking AMPARs eliminated responses to single stimuli only, and blocking mGluR1 eliminated responses to 1 s steps to 10–60 spk/s (Figure 5a and b, cell #3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Blocking mGluR2/3s shortened the delay between the step increases in MF stimulation and UBC firing rate increases.
source: In this cell, blocking mGluR2/3s shortened the delay between the step increases in MF stimulation and UBC firing rate increases (Figure 5a and b, cell #7), blocking AMPARs had very little effect, and blocking mGluR1s eliminated UBC responses.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Blocking AMPARs eliminated excitatory responses evoked by individual stimuli at 5 spk/s, 1 spk/s, and 2.5 spk/s stimuli.
source: Blocking AMPARs eliminated excitatory responses evoked by individual stimuli at 5 spk/s (Figure 5a–d), 1 spk/s, and 2.5 spk/s stimuli (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 5 and 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: For most UBCs, 1 s 10–60 spk/s MF stimulation evoked slow changes in UBC firing that remained prominent in the presence of mGluR2/3 and AMPAR antagonists and were eliminated by blocking mGluR1.
source: For most UBCs, 1 s 10–60 spk/s MF stimulation evoked slow changes in UBC firing that remained prominent in the presence of mGluR2/3 and AMPAR antagonists. These responses were eliminated by blocking mGluR1 (Figure 5a–d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Many UBCs showed clear increases in their excitatory response after suppression of mGluR2/3s.
source: Plotting the change in spikes evoked by each 1 s step for the successive application of antagonists revealed that many UBCs showed clear increases in their excitatory response after suppression of mGluR2/3s (Figure 5e and f), which were also evident in the heatmaps (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Suppression of AMPARs only mildly reduced the number of evoked spikes for most steps.
source: Suppression of AMPARs only mildly reduced the number of evoked spikes for most steps (Figure 5g), with 90% (9/10) of UBCs that showed increases in firing to the 60 spk/s step before suppression of AMPAR, still responding after (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The number of evoked spikes was close to zero for all UBCs after suppression of mGluR1.
source: However, the number of evoked spikes was close to zero for all UBCs after suppression of mGluR1 (Figure 5e and h).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: During smooth pursuit-like input patterns, mGluR1 is the main mediator of excitatory responses, while mGluR2/3 is the main mediator of inhibitory responses.
source: We conclude that, during smooth pursuit-like input patterns, mGluR1 is the main mediator of excitatory responses, while mGluR2/3 is the main mediator of inhibitory responses. and, additionally, reduces excitation overall throughout stimulation.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the results based on the pharmacological experiments.

claim: For low-rate inputs in fast UBCs, AMPARs mediate an additional excitatory response that preserves timing information of the input.
source: For low-rate inputs in fast UBCs, AMPARs mediate an additional excitatory response that preserves timing information of the input, while mGluR2/3s provide an analogous inhibitory response in slower UBCs.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the results based on the pharmacological experiments.

claim: mGluR2/3s provide an analogous inhibitory response in slower UBCs for low-rate inputs.
source: For low-rate inputs in fast UBCs, AMPARs mediate an additional excitatory response that preserves timing information of the input, while mGluR2/3s provide an analogous inhibitory response in slower UBCs.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the results based on the pharmacological experiments.

claim: The UBC population powerfully preprocesses MF inputs during realistic MF activation.
source: Our findings establish that the UBC population powerfully preprocesses MF inputs during realistic MF activation.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: UBCs simultaneously convey timing information, and a slow filtered version of the MF firing pattern that continuously varies across the population.
source: UBCs simultaneously convey timing information, and a slow filtered version of the MF firing pattern that continuously varies across the population (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the experimental findings and shown in Figure 6b.

claim: For many UBCs AMPARs convey timing information about MF firing by responding to single stimuli, short bursts, and individual stimuli during prolonged low-frequency MF activation.
source: We find that for many UBCs AMPARs covey timing information about MF firing by responding to single stimuli, short bursts, and individual stimuli during prolonged low-frequency MF activation (Figure 3, Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 3, 5, and 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: AMPARs primarily mediate responses to high frequency bursts of up to 5 stimuli, but as the burst duration increases their contribution diminishes and mGluR1s are the primary driver of increases in firing for most UBCs.
source: AMPARs primarily mediate responses to high frequency bursts of up to 5 stimuli, but as the burst duration increases their contribution diminishes and mGluR1s are the primary driver of increases in firing for most UBCs (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: A large fraction of the UBC population fire in response to each stimulus during 1–5 spk/s MF stimulation, and these responses are driven almost entirely by AMPARs.
source: A large fraction of the UBC population fire in response to each stimulus during 1–5 spk/s MF stimulation, and these responses are driven almost entirely by AMPARs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: AMPAR responses last up to 400ms, which is much longer than AMPA-mediated EPSCs observed at most synapses.
source: Although brief compared to UBC responses mediated by mGluR1s following prolonged bursts, AMPAR responses still last up to 400ms, which is much longer than AMPA-mediated EPSCs observed at most synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental observations.

claim: The slow time course of AMPAR responses is consistent with the properties of AMPAR EPSCs at MF-UBC synapses that arise from the ultrastructure of UBC synapses, the resulting slow glutamate signal, and the distinctive properties of the AMPARs present in UBCs.
source: This slow time course is consistent with the properties of AMPAR EPSCs at MF-UBC synapses that arise from the ultrastructure of UBC synapses, the resulting slow glutamate signal, and the distinctive properties of the AMPARs present in UBCs (Rossi et al., 1995; Kinney et al., 1997; van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014; Lu et al., 2017; Balmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The multiple phases of the AMPAR response evoked by 20 stimuli at 100 spk/s bursts likely reflect initial activation, desensitization during stimulation, and a large slow rebound current after stimulation as the prolonged presence of glutamate activates AMPARs as they recover from desensitization.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.
